items.lbText:
James Norton and Lucy Punch star as a youthful Mr and Mrs Claus in lively ad about shared moments as well as shopping

For years the “Christmas advert moment” has belonged to one brand. John Lewis’s syrupy commercials featuring piano ballads and tearjerker storylines have given the 160-year-old department store a cultural head start in the dash for festive profits.

This year, however, there’s one high-street rival with a sackful of tricks to make up the ground. Marks & Spencer has brought out the big guns – in the form of a topless Santa, played by the small-screen heart-throb James Norton .

The lively M&S Christmas ad has already drawn comparisons with John Lewis’s effort , which features Kristin Scott Thomas as a glamorous granny on the hunt to turn one room of her huge townhouse into a fun “gran cave”.

In the M&S corner Norton and Lucy Punch play a youthful Mr and Mrs Claus – with a lingering shot of Norton with his top off.

When John Lewis launched its advert this week, its portrayal of wealth was criticised, with a sprawling house and ungrateful grandchildren said to be out of touch with the wider mood of the nation.

But shots of Norton topless aside from an M&S white cotton towel have gone viral. Men’s Health magazine described him as a “shredded Santa”, saying his Saint Nick “leaves the traditional mince-pie physique looking a little dated”.

Gurjit Degun, the creativity and cultural editor at Campaign, a business magazine that covers advertising and marketing, described the M&S ad as “playful and tongue in cheek without being silly”.

M&S has combined its fashion, food, beauty and homeware strands into one campaign rather than individual adverts, a strategy it last used in 2017. Norton plays an undercover Santa who shaves off his beard so he can experience the buildup to Christmas incognito, while Punch is a snobbish Mrs Claus, similar to her character in Amandaland .

After the couple gatecrash a dinner party, swing by a children’s carol service and discover “picky bits”, the key takeaway from M&S is that Christmas is about shared moments rather than just big gifts. Although of course the advert is very much about shopping. Every element of it – from Punch’s pyjamas to that towel and the prawn cones Norton said he saw “hundreds” of during filming – is available to buy. Meanwhile, the main message derived from the John Lewis campaign is to give physical gifts rather than cold, hard cash.

Norton said the combination of a “playful, funny and reverent script” appealed to him. He is a “huge fan” of the advert’s director, Shannon Murphy, who has worked on shows including Killing Eve and Babyteeth.

“I trusted that Shannon would deliver on the tone,” he said. “She’s such a cool cat.” While he is usually “a sucker for a traditional tearjerker”, he believes the ad still captures the emotion of Christmas thanks to those family-and-friends moments that speak to “connection and joy”.

Punch said she liked the deliberately humorous script. “I don’t want any more Christmas tearjerkers,” she said. “I want fun and joy. Life is enough of a tearjerker, it’s fun to have something festive with a bit of a wink.”

In a tough consumer market, there is a lot weighing on the adverts’ success for the retailers. M&S is still trying to bounce back from a 2025 cyber hack that forced it to close its website for more than six weeks, costing it over £100m; John Lewis is trying to revive interest as it grapples with higher costs alongside a decline in consumer confidence .

Jonathan De Mello, the founder of JDM Retail consulting, describes the John Lewis strategy as smart, explaining that the casting of Scott Thomas reflected the type of customer the retailer was trying to appeal to.

“They are targeting a group that is fairly affluent,” he said. “They have a decent chunk of disposable income because they have paid off their mortgages.” However, this approach could “alienate the mass market”, he cautioned, as for a younger generation “it portrays a type of lifestyle that for many is unattainable”.

The M&S advert is a reflection of how the retailer has successfully turned its business around, De Mello said. “Before, there was a dichotomy between the food and the fashion, and now they are very much aligned. M&S now taps into the younger consumer psyche and this advert reflects this.”

items.lbText:
Bills have soared in rural state buffeted by tariffs and war in Iran – and Democrat Adam Hamilton’s stunning upset shows how deep economic frustrations run

L inda Olson always does her homework before voting – a trait she inherited from a family invested, and interested, in politics. Her father was a photographer who took portraits of political leaders in Washington, while her grandparents were farmers who cared deeply about their industry.

In 2024, Olson’s research led her to Donald Trump . She trusted that the then-former president would improve their economic realities in Junction City, Kansas – where she was born and raised – if he returned to the White House.

But two years later, life is just more expensive. Last winter, Olson was forced to spend $700 on medication while in between insurance plans, and skipped out on doses to stretch it out longer. Her grocery bills are unrecognizably high. And fuel prices are about a dollar per gallon more expensive than last year.

“I thought at the time that he was the better choice of what we had,” Olson said of Trump in 2024. Instead, he had been acting to “make himself richer instead of really helping the people”.

With frustrations like these looming large across the state, Kansans this week elected a Democrat, Adam Hamilton, to the US Senate for the first time in nearly a century. It was a stunning upset in what was, until recently, thought to be a reliably red stronghold.

“I’ve seen what Roger Marshall did over the eight years or so that he’s been doing this,” said Olson, of the defeated Republican senator. “And I thought, it’s time we get fresh blood up there.”

Hamilton won, in part, by flipping six counties that backed Trump in 2024 and Marshall in 2020 – a sign that, even in more remote, and traditionally conservative, areas, patience with Trump and the Republican party is wearing thin.

“Not everybody that voted for Trump is part of this cult of personality that Trump has tried to make the Republican party into,” said Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, located in one of those six flipped counties.

“There are certainly people in Kansas that are like that: they’re pretty conservative, but they’re not beholden to Trump. And so I think one of the things this election did is peel off those people.”

M ost of Kansas is made up of farmland, encompassing nearly 45m acres and employing nearly one in five Kansans. Pastures, dotted with grazing cows and their calves, hug the state’s highways. Junction City is surrounded by its famed toffee-colored prairies, so expansive that untouched grassland stretches out to the horizon on both sides of the interstate.

Kansans who ranch and farm here, in the most rural corners of the state, remain deeply Republican, according to Smith. But neighboring communities such as Junction City and Emporia, where he teaches, depend heavily on the agricultural economy and have felt the impact of the strains on farmers.

“The people that live here aren’t actually farmers,” he said. “And they’re more likely to swing over to the other party because the economy is really taking a beating.”

David Aguirre, a 25-year-old who was born and raised in Junction City, and works at a Mexican restaurant, El Patron Dos, said that when the rest of the county is suffering, so does his work.

“It has, like, a domino effect for families,” he said. “If they’re not doing their best, they’re not gonna come out to eat, and then that affects staff, and cooks, and so on.”

While grocery shopping on Wednesday afternoon, Janet Grimm, who considers herself an independent, lamented her rising bills. Everything she picked out from the aisles was tagged with a red and yellow “sale” sticker, a conscious choice she needs to make now.

Checking out with just a handful of items – eggs, chicken, some deli meat, two cucumbers and powdered sugar for the banana bread she was planning on making later that day – her total rang up to over $60.

Grimm voted for Hamilton, and felt hopefully that he would be able to improve the economy for people like her. “I really have faith that they’re going to do good,” she said.

H amilton – whose campaign slogan was “leading from the middle” – followed an increasingly reliable playbook in Kansas, Smith suggested, in which candidates position themselves as moderate and distant from the national Democratic party. In his victory speech on Tuesday, Hamilton emphasized to a packed room of supporters that he would seek greater collaboration between parties during his tenure, to “solve problems like it used to be”.

“I’m going to tell you a little secret. I want to become Jerry Moran’s best friend,” said Hamilton, referring to the state’s other senator – a Republican.

“For the rest of the United States, in deeply red Kansas, the heart of America, I want us to model what it looks like when thoughtful people actually work together to solve problems, instead of slinging mud at each other.”

Channeling his years as the pastor of a megachurch, Hamilton recounted the story of the Good Samaritan – in which a Samaritan stopped to help a man who was beaten on his way from Jerusalem to Jericho – as a way to illustrate the importance of Democrats and Republicans helping out one another.

“If Jesus were telling this parable to a room filled with Democrats , he’d say, ‘And there was a Republican who came along and stopped and helped the man,’” said Hamilton. “If he was talking to a room filled with Republicans, he’d say, ‘And there was a Democrat who came along and stopped.’”

Every county in Kansas shifted to vote more Democrat in this year’s Senate race. Still, many areas of the state remain staunchly Republican, and no moderate candidate is likely to change that, said Smith.

“It’s still a pretty conservative state,” he said. “Let’s not get too hasty here.”…

items.lbText:
Bank’s decision goes contrary to analysis from Office for Budget Responsibility that predicts lower inflation and little impetus for wage growth

Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%

An interest rate rise by the Bank of England to 4% is a big call when households are suffering from a second cost of living crisis in four years.

Many people will be incredulous when they hear of the decision to increase the cost of borrowing by 0.25 percentage points, looking around their neighbourhood for signs of a booming economy.

The official figures show the economy has proved resilient in response to the jump in oil and gas prices after the outbreak of war in Iran, but UK high streets are struggling and the underlying drivers of inflation are absent.

Most households are spending to stand still, whether it is on food, energy, holidays or leisure pursuits. Businesses are in much the same position. Like households, they have absorbed significant tax rises.

What the Bank’s policymakers believe is that despite all this, the energy price shock, being larger than first estimated, will surge through all parts of the economy, forcing up prices, encouraging a wave of wage demands that will, in turn, give inflation a second burst of life next year and the following year.

This analysis stands in contrast to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), which acts as the Treasury’s independent forecaster. The OBR was clear in evidence to parliament on Wednesday that there was little impetus for strong wages growth.

The OBR said that, rather than economic growth next year of 1.6% and a rise in inflation to 4.9%, as the Bank expects, it believes the economy will expand by just 1% in 2027 and that the consumer prices index (CPI) will peak at just 3.75%. Inflation hit 3.5% in September, official figures showed .

The OBR’s chief economist, David Miles, said one of the main reasons for this assessment was the state of UK businesses, which he judged to be quite weak.

He said they had absorbed a large slice of the rise in energy and fuel costs, and their profit margins had plummeted on average as a result. Where once margins averaged 13% to 14%, the latest figures show they have fallen to 10% to 11%.

He said there would be little appetite to pay high wage settlements and the imperative would be to rebuild margins.

The wider economic situation is also very different from the previous crisis in 2022, when the country was coming out of the pandemic and dealing with the onset of the Ukraine war.

Back then, households were awash with lockdown savings that they wanted to spend, and firms were struggling to hire enough staff, leading to intense competition for workers and a spike in wages.

Today, savings are low and households bear the scars of four years of high inflation.

What sectors of the economy are making hay in 2026? Retailers and hospitality businesses are suffering, transport companies are battered by high costs and the charity sector is facing widespread financial difficulties. Vacancies are low, suggesting that firms have no need to employ more people.

Businesses in better-performing sectors such as banking and oil and gas also show little appetite for big wage increases. Banks are using artificial intelligence to shed staff .

The deputy director of the British Chambers of Commerce, David Bharier, said he was dismayed by the decision.

“So far, there is little sign of the wage-price spiral the Bank is looking to guard against. Unemployment is higher than in 2022, the labour market is looser and our research shows AI adoption accelerating rapidly – with some of the deepest users more likely to expect headcount reductions,” he said.

“After a budget which gave businesses little incentive to invest, and with borrowing costs already high, it is economic growth that will pay the premium.”

The Bank’s own survey of businesses and a separate report from its regional agents indicate “that wage and price expectations have moved little since September”.

It means Threadneedle Street policymakers judge that responses to their own business review will prove inaccurate and wages will jump.

The Bank judged that households’ and firms’ “attentiveness” to rising inflation was high and “there was a risk wage settlements would be higher than businesses expect”.

When the government says it is constrained by the bond markets from spending more to help consumers, there is a scenario looming in which ministers and the central bank, to meet their individual mandates, effectively crush the prospects for economic growth.

John Healey will say, as he did at the dispatch box last week, that he needs to restrict borrowing and adhere to his fiscal rules. Meanwhile, the bank will be busy making sure it cracks down on inflationary pressures it believes are on the way, even if policymakers cannot see them quite yet.

items.title: Was Elon Musk the US midterms' biggest loser? – Stateside with Kai and Carter
items.author: Hosted by Carter Sherman and Kai Wright with Blake Montgomery . Produced by Anabel Bacon and Monica Espitia, engineered by Ivan Kuraev, executive producer Rachel Humphreys
items.content:
The tech industry spent big on the midterms, but it turned out to be a poor investment. Elon Musk poured a staggering $446m dollars into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, but his efforts didn’t pay off. Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates. Carter Sherman and Kai Wright are joined by the Guardian’s US tech editor, Blake Montgomery, to ask what the ‘blue tsunami’ will mean for Musk and the wider tech industry. Future brightens for US developers in particular after election when voters rejected Trump’s war on clean energy

After years as collateral damage in Donald Trump’s war on climate action, the Democrats’ sweeping triumph in the US midterm elections has emerged as a victory for the global renewable energy industry too.

Across the world’s financial centres the market value of renewable energy developers climbed as the election results confirmed the Republicans had lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives.

For the world’s largest offshore wind developer, Ørsted , the shift in power could spell a reprieve from the White House’s assaults on the Danish company’s multibillion-dollar offshore wind investments off the north-east US coast.

Ørsted’s market value jumped by almost 10% within hours of the Democratic victory, before closing nearly 5% higher. The share price of other European renewables companies active in the US also climbed. Portugal’s EDP Renewables and the French utility Engie rose by more than 3%. Shares in Germany’s RWE added about 1%.

The clean energy market rally marks a modest boost for Ørsted, which has lost more than 70% of its market value since Trump returned to the White House in 2025 and resumed his salvoes against the industry as it struggled against fast-rising interest rates and supply chain pressures.

The White House has levelled multiple stop-orders against Ørsted’s Revolution Wind project since the re-election of Trump, a vocal supporter of the fossil fuel industry , who has repeatedly opposed the development of “ ugly, costly and inefficient ” windfarms in the US and abroad.

The impact has been chilling for the burgeoning US renewables sector too. The US is home to renewable energy projects with a combined capacity of 388 gigawatts, or enough to power more than 83m American homes. The sector also directly employs more than 400,000 people across the country.

This fleet of wind, solar, hydro and geothermal power projects has made up about 30% of the electricity generated across the US this year – well below the 50% share across the EU and China’s 40%.

While there is no binding US-wide clean energy target, there are 24 states, plus the District of Columbia, with plans to achieve 100% clean electricity or net zero carbon emissions between 2035 and 2050.

But there has been growing disquiet over whether the forecast surge in electricity-hungry AI datacentres poses a threat to green targets by increasing the US reliance on gas power plants – and energy costs.

“This was unquestioningly an energy election,” said Brenda Shaffer, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global Energy Center. Rising concerns over energy costs and the looming impact of datacentres on energy supplies had played a key role in Republican defeat, she said.

The Democrats’ decisive control of the US House of Representatives and its majority in the Senate may reduce the risk of further political interference and bring fresh confidence to the US renewable energy industry, according to market analysts.

The Democratic house would be able to block further repeals of solar and wind tax credits, said Claudio Galimberti, the chief economist at the consultancy Rystad Energy. Battery storage credits would also now have a stronger defender in budget negotiations, and the administration’s roughly $4bn in offshore wind lease buybacks would face greater scrutiny, he added.

While it was too early to call this a turning point for US offshore wind, said Tancrede Fulop, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar in the Netherlands, the election outcome might lower the risk of further regulatory disruption and provide a more stable backdrop for projects under development.

“For companies that have spent the past few years dealing with regulatory delays and shifting political priorities, a more supportive backdrop should provide some much-needed confidence around projects already under development,” he said.

This in turn may ease investor jitters around regulatory uncertainty and support confidence in future project returns, according to analysts at Barclays, which could make new US renewable energy projects cheaper to finance.

The future was even brighter for developers hoping to build new onshore renewable energy projects, including batteries, which are typically decided at state level, said Shaffer.

A string of Republican states have turned blue – including Texas, Maine, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and North and South Carolina – potentially ushering in greater support for clean energy investments.

The “blue wave” had made it clear that “affordable, reliable power is a priority”, according to Jason Grumet, the chief executive of the American Clean Power Association (ACP). “And our industry is ready to deliver it.”

items.title: Lab-grown meat was supposed to save the world. What happened?
items.author: Erin Somers
items.content:
We were promised a panacea for the climate crisis and a way to save our food system. So why is nobody firing up the chicken vats? I went to find out

On 5 August 2013, a man and a woman ate a burger. Not just any burger: a world-historic burger, made from cattle cells grown in a laboratory by Mark Post, a professor of vascular physiology at Maastricht University in the Netherlands. The burger had taken two years to produce and cost €250,000 (about £210,000 at the time), money furnished by the Google co-founder Sergey Brin. Now it was being tasted in public for the first time at Riverside Studios in London, at an event attended by 200 members of the press and livestreamed to thousands.

To make this particular burger, Post had extracted stem cells from the shoulder muscle of a living cow, then cultivated them in plastic containers filled with a nutrient-rich supplement called foetal bovine serum, which is derived from cow foetuses. The cells eventually became 20,000 strands of tissue, which in turn became a single 140g patty. Post believed that beef produced this way had the potential to dramatically reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and slow the climate crisis. Raising cattle for consumption requires massive amounts of land and water – and massive amounts of feed grown at a high environmental cost. He projected that global demand for meat would soon outstrip our ability to produce it the old-fashioned way, at which point our food systems would become unsustainable. But that didn’t have to mean a mass recalibration of our consumption habits or a global shift away from red meat. Post and his team had found another way.

items.title: ‘It’s just vape shops, nail shops, charity shops’: can anything save the British high street?
items.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
items.content:
It’s 20 years since Jo and Richard Hill bought anything in Rotherham town centre. Why have they and so many locals abandoned it for the nearest retail park – and what would it take to change their minds?

On 22 May 1987, retail history was made in Rotherham. Parkgate Retail World, thought at the time to be the UK’s largest open-air shopping centre, welcomed shoppers for some one-stop retail therapy. The official opening was marked in swanky fashion with a “breathtaking” display from Marlboro’s red-and-white branded biplanes, followed by a “spectacular” laser show, the first in South Yorkshire. Helen Worth – Coronation Street’s Gail Platt – cut the ribbon before jovial local people jostled to fill their car boots with goods from Comet, Jolly Giant and Poundstretcher.

Almost 40 years on, the razzle is a bit less dazzling. Parkgate, as the retail park is called now, looks like any large big-box outdoor shopping centre you might find on urban fringes. There’s a Primark, a Sports Direct and a Matalan, plus (of course) a Frankie & Benny’s. Shoppers still seem to love it. “I think it’s ideal. It’s got everything here,” says Robert Gordon. The 66-year-old retired factory production manager had popped to Pets at Home to get a cupcake and toy for his dog Bruno’s fourth birthday.

Access to our £37,000 deposit in a savings account is restricted after a ‘routine security review’

My wife’s Revolut account was frozen in what it calls a “routine security review” over a week ago. Nothing has been requested from her – no documents, the source of funds, or ID – yet, as a result, our house deposit of £37,000 in a joint savings account is also restricted.

We’re approaching the completion of our property purchase and have given notice on our rental home. Direct debits are bouncing and we’re concerned about our credit records.

At one point Revolut also restricted my personal account, so we effectively had no access to any money. We keep being given deadlines for the restrictions to be lifted which are missed, and call centre staff, when we can get through, have little ability to find out what’s happening, or make anything happen. XWF , Oxfordshire

Banks have legal powers, under anti-money-laundering regulations, to freeze accounts if a sudden windfall, overseas payment or unusual activity raises concerns. They are not required to warn customers or explain if they suspect foul play, although customers can complain to the Financial Ombudsman Service if they believe a bank acted unfairly.

There’s no suggestion foul play was suspected in your wife’s case and things progressed swiftly after I got involved. Accounts were reinstated, nearly three weeks after being suspended, and your wife was offered £175 as a goodwill gesture. Revolut says regulatory constraints prevented it explaining. “We’re sorry our review process took longer than usual, and our communication didn’t reach its usual standards, particularly given the inconvenience during an important life moment,” it says.

items.lbText:
He needs a dialysis machine to survive, but on a flight it was first damaged, then it was lost

My father suffers from terminal renal failure and relies on a highly specific dialysis machine every night to survive. British Airways’ check-in staff twice insisted on checking this fragile 20kg lifeline into the aircraft hold where it was first damaged, then lost.

When his outbound flight arrived at Heathrow, it was returned broken resulting in a frantic search for a loan unit and hours spent in A&E so my father’s blood could be monitored. On the return flight to Rome, the machine could not be found. My parents waited until 2am before being told to go home without the equipment that keeps my father alive.

He had to borrow another unit from a hospital. His was finally delivered three days later with the protective case unsealed and critical internal components disconnected.

The sheer terror and stress of missing a treatment, not knowing if the A&E could accommodate him in time, and fearing that his health had already been severely compromised, was indescribable.

British Airways has missed all deadlines to address our complaint and is now ignoring our correspondence. DL , London

Your father did not need to use the fragile unit during the flight but was concerned, rightly as it turned out, it might suffer damage in the hold.

BA, in common with most airlines, allows vital medical equipment to travel for free along with its owner, provided it does not exceed the dimensions of cabin baggage. It’s essential for safety reasons that belongings can be stowed under a seat or an overhead locker.

Your father’s device was too large, and I believe it was reasonable for BA to check it into the hold if the flight was full. If, however, there were spare seats, it could have allowed it to travel on one. It has since told you a seat could have been bought.

The real shocker is that such vital kit was mishandled not once, but twice. The impact on your father could have been grave had loan units not been found. BA’s response was, at best, cavalier.

When you wrote to me, a month had passed since your initial complaint and you’d heard nothing besides auto-generated acknowledgments.

The company got its act together when I questioned its attitude. An operative called you to apologise and it managed, at last, to reply to your emails. However, you are unimpressed by its offer of £300 in e-vouchers to, in its words, “put things right”. I’ve suggested it convert this into cash and consider a sum that better reflects the impact on your father. It told me it will be in touch to discuss a “gesture”.
